A hypothesis framework linking the menopausal transition, sleep and brain waste clearance: Insights from experimental models.
papers.abstract: The menopausal transition is increasingly recognized as a neuroendocrine transition with implications for brain health, sleep, cognition and vulnerability to neurodegenerative disease. Fluctuating and declining ovarian hormones coincide with sleep disruption, vasomotor symptoms, cognitive complaints, neuroinflammation and altered blood-brain barrier integrity. Current preclinical models each capture selected components of the menopause transition and provide essential mechanistic insights into the effect of ovarian hormone loss on the brain. Across these models, endocrine change is associated with impairments in hippocampal and prefrontal-dependent cognition, altered sleep-wake regulation, vascular dysfunction, glial activation, disrupted synaptic and mitochondrial homeostasis and exacerbation of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease-like pathology. An emerging but understudied mechanism linking menopause, sleep and neurodegeneration is the glymphatic system, a sleep-dependent brain waste clearance pathway. This review synthesises current evidence to highlight how menopause-related sleep disruption, vascular dysfunction, neuroinflammation and potential alterations in brain-waste clearance may converge to shape cognitive ageing and neurodegenerative disease risk.

papers.title: Acoustic stimuli-enhanced environmental enrichment remodulates cortical processing of sound azimuth in adult female rats.
papers.abstract: Acoustic stimuli-enhanced environmental enrichment (AEE) has been shown to significantly facilitate the behavioral and neuronal processing of sound by promoting plasticity in the auditory system. However, the mechanisms through which acoustic stimulation contributes to enrichment-induced effects remain largely unexplored. Here we found that AEE exposure during adulthood significantly improved the sound-azimuth discrimination abilities of female rats compared to age-matched naïve controls. Furthermore, AEE enhanced the sound-azimuth selectivity of neurons in the primary auditory cortex. These changes in the behavioral and cortical processing of sound azimuth were accompanied by an increase in the density of cortical parvalbumin-labeled (PV+) inhibitory interneurons. Interestingly, the rats reared in an identical enriched condition but without extra sound exposure also exhibited sharper cortical azimuth tuning and more cortical PV+ interneurons compared to the naïve rats. However, the post-rearing effects in these rats were less pronounced than those observed in the AEE rats, indicating an additional contribution of acoustic stimulation to enrichment-induced changes in the mature auditory cortex. Together, these findings provide compelling evidence for the significant influence of AEE on behavioral and cortical processing of sound azimuth. They suggest that AEE is an effective paradigm for promoting experience-dependent plasticity in the auditory system, even beyond the traditionally recognized critical period.

papers.title: From features to digital biomarkers: EEG-fNIRS classification pipelines for brain monitoring.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) are widely used for noninvasive brain monitoring in clinical and cognitive applications, where machine learning-based classification has become increasingly prevalent. Alongside algorithmic advances, a growing body of literature reports signal-derived metrics as digital biomarkers; however, their interpretation, validity, and comparability remain strongly dependent on target definition, processing pipelines, and evaluation practices. This review provides a structured overview of EEG- and fNIRS-based classification studies, with a particular focus on signal processing workflows and biomarker extraction. The reviewed literature is organized around key stages of the analytical pipeline, including target formulation, data preprocessing, feature extraction, and validation. Common feature families-spanning spectral, temporal, connectivity-based, network-level, and hemodynamic representations-are summarized and discussed in relation to their typical applications and limitations. The main contribution is an evidence-based distinction between signal features and credible candidate biomarkers. Reliability, analytical robustness, external generalization, and interpretability are considered within the intended context of use. Clinical utility is assessed separately from predictive performance. Across 117 primary studies, most measures remained candidate biomarkers; only four studies were assigned to independent clinical validation, with qualifications, and none evaluated clinical utility.

papers.title: Choroid plexus volume as a marker of chronotherapeutic responsiveness in major depressive disorder.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythm disruption is a core feature of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). The choroid plexus (ChP), a circadian-regulated structure involved in cerebrospinal fluid production and immune signalling, has been previously associated with depression and may undergo structural changes in response to chronotherapeutics. The study included 25 patients with MDD and 25 matched healthy controls who underwent MRI. Patients received total sleep deprivation plus light therapy (TSD + LT), consisting of three 36-hour sleep deprivation cycles, each separated by a night of recovery sleep. LT was administered for 30 min every morning. Depressive symptoms, sleep quality, and chronotype were assessed through Beck's Depression Inventory (BDI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ), respectively. ChP volumes were extracted with FreeSurfer and normalized for intracranial volume. Effects of chronotherapeutics were assessed on BDI, PSQI, and ChP volumes, with treatment response as a between-subject factor. The efficacy of treatment was also investigated stratifying for chronotype. Also, group differences in ChP volume and associations with sleep and BDI scores were explored. TSD + LT reduced depressive symptoms and improved sleep quality, with changes in PSQI associated with symptom improvement. Eveningness predicted greater depressive symptom reduction. At baseline, responders already exhibited larger left ChP volume than controls. Following treatment, a treatment × response interaction emerged for right ChP volume, showing a significant reduction in responders. Finally, reductions in both right and left ChP volumes predicted clinical improvement, and sleep quality improvement predicted right ChP volume reduction. This is the first study showing that chronotherapy modulates ChP structure in MDD, suggesting a link between circadian dysregulation and ChP enlargement proportional to clinical improvement and predicted by sleep amelioration. ChP volume may represent a biomarker of treatment responsiveness and circadian realignment.

papers.title: Enhanced functional connectivity in right precuneus after high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in Parkinson's disease patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain.
papers.abstract: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) can relieve chronic musculoskeletal pain (MSP) in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 43 PD patients with MSP were randomly assigned to received 10 sessions of neuronavigated 10-Hz rTMS (n=22) or sham stimulation (n=21) over the bilateral primary motor cortex (M1). Clinical assessments were performed at baseline (T0), after the tenth session (T1), and at 1-month (T2) and 3-month (T3) follow-up; functional MRI (fMRI) was acquired at T0 and T1. In the rTMS group, compared to T0, King's Parkinson's Disease Pain Scale (KPPS) and Visual Analog Scale scores decreased significantly at T1, T2, and T3 (p < 0.05). MDS-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) III, Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA), Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD), and Parkinson's Disease Sleep Scale (PDSS) scores were significantly lower at T1 and T2 than at T0 (p < 0.05), but not at T3 (p > 0.05). No significant correlations were found between KPPS and MDS-UPDRS III, HAMA, HAMD, or PDSS scores (p > 0.05) alterations in the rTMS group. fMRI revealed that patients exhibited decreased amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations in the left cuneus and enhanced functional connectivity between the left cuneus and the right precuneus after rTMS treatment. The sham group showed no significant changes in clinical scores or fMRI. High-frequency rTMS over bilateral M1 was associated with improvement of MSP in PD, accompanied by reduced local neural activity in the left cuneus and enhanced connectivity between the left cuneus and the right precuneus. These findings are preliminary and hypothesis generating.

papers.title: EEG Microstate Alterations and Their Association with Cognitive Performance in Late-Onset Epilepsy of Unknown Etiology: Comparison with Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment is common in late-onset epilepsy of unknown etiology (LOEU), but its electrophysiological correlates and relationship to Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain unclear. We compared resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) microstate dynamics among LOEU, AD, and cognitively normal (CN) groups and examined their associations with cognitive performance. Eyes-closed 32-channel resting-state EEG recordings were analyzed from 60 patients with LOEU, 65 with AD, and 60 CN participants. Four canonical microstate classes (A-D) were identified. Group differences in microstate parameters were tested with false discovery rate correction. Associations with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores were examined using multivariable interaction models adjusted for age, sex, education, and cerebral small vessel disease burden. Microstate B duration was longer in LOEU and AD than in CN (Holm-adjusted p=0.011 and 0.016), whereas microstate C occurrence was lower in both patient groups (p=0.001 and 0.018). Microstate D duration was longer in LOEU than in CN and AD (both p=0.038). For microstate A duration, the group interaction survived false discovery rate correction for MMSE (q=0.0255) but not MoCA (q=0.122). In LOEU, longer microstate A duration was associated with lower MoCA and MMSE scores. Pairwise slope comparisons were more negative in LOEU than in CN for both outcomes, whereas LOEU-AD slope differences were not significant. LOEU showed altered resting-state EEG microstate dynamics that partly overlapped with those observed in AD, alongside a group difference in microstate D duration. Microstate A duration was associated with cognitive performance in LOEU, although this association did not significantly differ from that observed in AD. These findings support further investigation of EEG microstates as electrophysiological correlates of cognitive dysfunction in LOEU while also highlighting overlap with AD.

papers.title: Altered directional brain-heart interactions across resting states and frequency bands in schizophrenia.
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia is associated with abnormalities in cortical activity and autonomic regulation, but directional brain-heart interaction (BHI) across resting states and frequency bands remains unclear. Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) and electrocardiography (ECG) were recorded simultaneously in 33 medicated men with schizophrenia and 29 healthy men during eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions. Directional BHI was assessed across two coupling directions, two cardiac frequency components, and five EEG frequency bands. Global-average and spatial cluster-based permutation analyses were performed, with family-wise error rate correction across all 40 predefined BHI features. Compared with healthy controls, patients with schizophrenia showed higher theta, alpha, and beta EEG power during eyes-open rest and higher theta and alpha EEG power during eyes-closed rest after false discovery rate correction. Cardiac low-frequency (LF) and high-frequency (HF) spectral power did not differ significantly between groups. During eyes-open rest, patients showed lower global-average brain-to-heart high-frequency (BtH-HF) coupling across all five EEG bands (global family-wise error rate-corrected p = 0.0151-0.0349; Hedges' g = -0.911 to -0.841). This finding was supported by spatial cluster analysis and multitaper sensitivity analysis. No eyes-closed BtH-HF effects survived global correction. Although four eyes-open heart-to-brain (HtB) clusters were initially significant under the fixed-order model, none survived the Bayesian information criterion-based order sensitivity analysis. No significant Condition × Group interaction was detected across the five BtH-HF features. Schizophrenia was associated with reduced eyes-open BtH-HF coupling across EEG bands, indicating altered statistical brain-heart coupling.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Fatty Acid Oxidation Dysregulation in Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease: Mechanistic Roles and Emerging Diagnostic and Therapeutic Advances.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is a chronic metabolic liver disorder driven by the convergent effects of obesity, insulin resistance, lipid overload, gut-liver axis disruption, and immune inflammation. Mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation is central to the disposal of excess fatty acids and the maintenance of hepatocellular energy homeostasis; under sustained metabolic stress, however, this process can shift from an adaptive response to a molecular hub for incomplete oxidation, oxidative injury, inflammatory amplification, and fibrotic progression. This review examines fatty acid uptake and activation, carnitine-dependent transport, sequential β-oxidation, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, electron transfer, mitochondrial quality control, and immunometabolic crosstalk, and explains how diet, circadian disruption, aging, gut dysbiosis, drug exposure, and genetic susceptibility destabilize oxidative homeostasis through defined molecular pathways. From a translational perspective, we propose a functional-endotype framework that integrates imaging, acylcarnitine profiling, lipidomics, oxidative-damage markers, inflammatory and fibrotic indices, and genetic risk to guide stratified interventions targeting thyroid hormone signaling, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors, incretin pathways, bile-acid signaling, fibroblast growth factors, energy-sensing networks, and precision nanomedicine.

papers.title: Using hip-worn accelerometer non-wear time to assess sleep duration and sleep midpoint.
papers.abstract: We sought to validate non-wear time of accelerometers worn on the hip for all waking hours as an estimate of sleep duration and midpoint. If valid, this may allow research studies to leverage previously collected physical activity data for sleep research. In 2019-2023, 21,325 Cancer Prevention Study-3 participants (mean age 58 years, SD=9.8) were provided a hip-worn accelerometer and sleep diaries for a week. Time in bed (TIB) was defined as the duration of non-wear time between two consecutive wear days (e.g. wear on Monday and Tuesday correspond to Monday night sleep). A total of 17,855 participants had at least 3 weekday and 1 weekend sleep measurements. Bland-Altman plots compared TIB and midpoint calculated from accelerometer non-wear and from sleep diaries. Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated for TIB to assess convergent validity, and a Two One-Sided Test (TOST) was calculated for midpoint to assess equivalence (± 15 minutes). Participants were mostly non-Hispanic white (87%) and female (77%). On average, TIB was 41.1 (SD=44.6) minutes longer on weekdays (r = 0.72) and 41.3 (SD=61.0) minutes longer on weekend days (r = 0.67) compared to sleep diary. Accelerometry sleep midpoint was 1.3 minutes earlier compared to diary on weekdays and 1.6 minutes later on weekends (TOST p-value < 0.01). TIB calculated from non-wear time of hip accelerometry demonstrated convergent validity with sleep duration assessed from sleep diary. Midpoint based on non-wear time was equivalent to sleep diary.

papers.title: Spatial-Frequency-Dependent Temporal Dynamics of Orientation Ensemble Representation.
papers.abstract: Average representation refers to the rapid extraction of the central tendency from a set of stimuli by the visual system. However, whether this efficient process relies on specific spatial frequency (SF) information remains poorly understood. To investigate the roles of low spatial frequency (LSF) and high spatial frequency (HSF) information in orientation ensemble averaging and the underlying temporal dynamics, we conducted two experiments combining behavioral and electroencephalographic (EEG) measures. Experiment 1 examined the effects of SF and visual field location on mean orientation judgments. Behavioral results indicated that LSF ensembles yielded superior accuracy and shorter reaction times compared to HSF ensembles, with performance further enhanced in the peripheral versus central visual field. To characterize the underlying temporal dynamics of ensemble processing, Experiment 2 focused on the peripheral field and utilized a neural adaptation paradigm in which the adapted and control test ensembles were matched in numerosity and spatial configuration. Electrophysiological results revealed a sequential processing trajectory: the LSF condition initially elicited a significant neural adaptation effect at the early C1 stage, followed by an HSF-elicited adaptation effect at the P1 stage. Finally, at the late P3 stage, the LSF condition exhibited a repetition enhancement effect. These findings suggest that orientation ensemble representation follows a spatial-frequency-dependent, coarse-fine-refine multistage dynamic pattern. Specifically, early LSF information facilitates a rapid, coarse holistic estimate; subsequently, HSF information contributes fine-grained details; and ultimately, the representation may be refined or calibrated through a late-stage process that may involve updating early LSF-based predictions.

papers.title: Time-Restricted Eating and Blood Pressure: Disentangling the Components of a Multidimensional Intervention.
papers.abstract: Time-restricted eating (TRE) has emerged as a promising chrononutritional strategy for improving cardiometabolic health, with human and experimental evidence suggesting beneficial effects on blood pressure (BP). However, attributing these effects specifically to meal timing remains challenging because TRE is not a single physiological exposure. Restricting the eating window may simultaneously modify fasting duration, circadian timing, energy balance, diet quality and nutritional composition, and body-weight dynamics, each of which may independently or interactively influence BP regulation. Interpretation is further complicated by how and when BP is assessed, particularly because BP is an intrinsically circadian phenotype. We propose a multidimensional framework that distinguishes these interconnected biological components from the methodological dimension of BP assessment. Disentangling them is essential to determine whether meal timing itself exerts an intrinsic antihypertensive effect and under which metabolic and circadian conditions such an effect emerges.

papers.title: Associations of short and long sleep duration with multiple adverse health outcomes among ageing adults in South Africa.
papers.abstract: The aim of this study was to assess the longitudinal associations between short and long sleep duration with multiple adverse health outcomes (mortality, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, functional limitations, depressive symptoms, loneliness, posttraumatic stress (PTSD) symptoms, impaired cognition, dynapenia, addominal obesity, dynapenic abdominal obesity, and general obesity) among community-residents 40 years and older, also broken down by sex. Data from three waves of the "Health and Ageing in Africa: A Longitudinal Study of an INDEPTH Community in South Africa (HAALSI)" (2015-2022) were utilized. There were 10483 observations of people who were 40 years of age or older. The American National Sleep Foundation was used to measure self-reported sleep duration. The association between sleep duration and 7-year mortality was assessed using hazard ratios. The longitudinal relationships between short and long sleep duration (using normal or recommended sleep length as a reference) and unfavorable health outcomes were estimated using linear, conditional, and multinomial logistic fixed effects (FE) regressions. This study showed an association between short sleep duration and mortality, hypertension, depressive symptoms, and cardiovascular disease, while there were no significant associations between short sleep duration and diabetes, functional limitations, loneliness, PTSD symptoms, impaired cognition, dynapenia, abdominal obesity, dynapenic abdominal obesity and general obesity. Furthermore, this study found an association between long sleep duration and functional limitations, depressive symptoms, loneliness, PTSD symptoms, impaired or lower cognition, dynapenia, abdominal obesity, dynapenic abdominal obesity and general obesity, while there were no significant associations between long sleep duration and mortality, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and diabetes. Short sleep duration was associated with four and long sleep duration with nine adverse health outcomes. The results can be applied to health literacy and education initiatives to promote getting adequate sleep, which is a crucial aspect of total sleep health. Future studies from other countries are recommended.

papers.title: Sex-related differences in subjective outcomes of mandibular advancement device treatment in adults with obstructive sleep apnea.
papers.abstract: To assess short-term sex-related differences in subjective outcomes of mandibular advancement device (MAD) treatment among obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) patients. This prospective longitudinal cohort study included OSA patients referred for MAD treatment at an academic dental clinic between April 2017 and August 2024. Baseline characteristics included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), and patient-reported OSA-related symptoms. Follow-up evaluations documented OSA-related symptoms, treatment adherence and side effects. Sex-related differences were assessed using Mann-Whitney U test, chi-square test, and repeated logistic regression model. This study included 460 patients (317 [68.9%] males; median [interquartile range] age = 50 [38-59] years, BMI = 26.3 [24.2-29.0] kg/m2, and AHI = 14.9 [9.4-21.4] events/hour). At baseline, females were older, while BMI and AHI did not differ significantly between sexes. Both sexes most frequently reported snoring and daytime fatigue, but females reported more daytime fatigue (P = .05) and breathing pauses during sleep (P = .04) than males. At follow-up, all symptoms decreased (P < .01), without significant sex-related differences. Adherence was similar between sexes, but females more frequently reported difficulty keeping the MAD in the mouth (P < .01) and dry mouth (P = .01). Age-stratified analyses showed no significant differences in baseline symptoms, symptom improvement, adherence, or side effects. MAD treatment was associated with reductions in subjective OSA-related symptoms in both sexes, without significant sex-related differences. However, females reported more fatigue and breathing pauses at baseline, and more side effects than males, highlighting sex-related differences in subjective treatment experiences.

papers.title: Identifying symptom-level drivers of the relationship between sleep health and depression.
papers.abstract: The present study examined which components of sleep health and depressive symptom domains contributed most strongly to the sleep-depression relationship in young adults. Young adults (n = 201) wore an actigraph for five nights and completed the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale (CES-D). Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) examined the multivariate association between sleep health (duration, regularity, timing, and efficiency) and CES-D (depressed affect, positive affect, somatic symptoms, interpersonal distress) domains. Covariate-adjusted linear regressions were then used to explore pairwise associations. The CCA identified a significant multivariate association between sleep health and depressive symptoms. Sleep timing and regularity contributed most strongly to the sleep canonical variate, while somatic symptoms and positive affect contributed most strongly to the depression canonical variate. In follow-up linear regressions, later sleep timing was associated with increased somatic symptoms after covariate adjustment and correction for multiple comparisons. Later sleep schedules may be particularly relevant to specific domains of depressive symptomatology in young adults.

papers.title: Psychosocial impacts of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19: insights from a longitudinal cohort.
papers.abstract: To characterize subjective stress in a previously hospitalized Neuropsychiatric Post-Acute Sequelae of COVID-19 (NP-PASC) cohort in New York City by examining its distribution, patterns, and associations with psychosocial and cognitive measures. This longitudinal study conducted a 3-4 year follow-up of moderate to severe COVID-19 survivors with NP-PASC, using the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), Urban Life Stress Scale (ULSS), and Everyday Discrimination Scale (EDS) to assess chronic stress. Associations with DSM-5 symptom domains, PSQI, UCLA Loneliness, ECog, and AD8 were analyzed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, ANOVA, chi-squared tests, and multivariate linear regression (p < 0.05). K-means clustering on standardized PSS scores identified PSS score strata (low, intermediate, high). All analyses were conducted in R version 4.3.2. Among 87 participants (mean age = 54, SD = 14), mean PSS scores for the low, intermediate, and high stress clusters were 7.08, 16.8, and 26.7, respectively. Higher perceived stress was associated with loneliness (β = 0.20, p < 0.001) and poor sleep (β = 0.34, p = 0.05). PSS scores increased by 2.07 points over time (p = 0.013), with greater increases among Hispanic (3.88, p = 0.026) and English-speaking (3.33, p = 0.008) participants. ULSS scores were higher among Spanish speakers (6.43, p = 0.017) and Hispanic/Other participants (9.5 vs. Black, p = 0.009). Discrimination experiences varied significantly by race, ethnicity, and language. Findings underscore the importance of integrating culturally sensitive, context-informed stress assessments into NP-PASC care to identify at-risk individuals and support recovery.

papers.title: Simultaneous EEG - fMRI study of brain activity during the autobiographical memory task in depressed patients with suicidal ideation.
papers.abstract: Over-general autobiographical memory (OGM) refers to the tendency to recall personal experiences vaguely rather than as specific incidents. OGM serves as a significant risk factor for suicidal ideation in depressed patients and may represent a novel target for early warning and intervention. However, differences in neural function during autobiographical memory retrieval among depressed patients with suicidal ideation, depressed patients without suicidal ideation, and healthy controls remain incompletely understood. We conducted an autobiographical memory test (AMT) using simultaneous EEG-fMRI measurements in 29 healthy controls (HC), 25 depressed patients without suicidal ideation (NSI), and 20 depressed patients with suicidal ideation (SI). The AMT comprised two stages: construction and elaboration, with the elaboration stage fixed at 10 s per trial. The SI group exhibited a significant reduction in specific autobiographical memories and took more time to construct these memories. During the memory construction stage, the SI group showed notably lower activation in left hemisphere regions, including the Medial Superior Frontal Gyrus (SFGmed), Calcarine (CAL), and Middle Frontal Gyrus (MFG), compared to both HC and NSI groups. Exploratory analyses controlling for depressive severity suggested that activation in the SFGmed, but not the CAL or MFG, remained specifically associated with suicidal ideation. During the memory elaboration stage, conventional fMRI analysis revealed significant group differences in five left-hemisphere regions (inferior frontal gyrus [orbital part], superior frontal gyrus, angular gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, and supplementary motor area), but these differences did not distinguish SI from NSI. However, EEG-informed fMRI analysis indicated that activation in the left hemisphere regions-Angular Gyrus, Superior Frontal Gyrus, SFGmed, and Supplementary Motor Area-was significantly reduced in the SI group compared to both the NSI and HC groups. Reduced activation levels in the Medial Superior Frontal Gyrus, Superior Frontal Gyrus, Middle Frontal Gyrus, Angular Gyrus, and Calcarine in the left hemisphere during autobiographical memory retrieval in depressed patients may be associated with the neural mechanisms linked to suicidal ideation. These findings may inform early identification and intervention strategies for suicide risk.

papers.title: Identification of circadian rhythm-related diagnostic biomarkers and immune subtypes in allergic rhinitis based on WGCNA and machine learning approaches.
papers.abstract: Allergic rhinitis (AR) is a common chronic inflammatory disease characterized by dysregulated immune responses and pronounced circadian rhythm disturbances. However, the molecular mechanisms linking circadian rhythm-related genes (CRRGs) to AR pathogenesis and immune heterogeneity remain insufficiently understood. Public microarray datasets (GSE75011 and GSE43523) were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between AR patients and healthy controls were identified using the limma package. Circadian rhythm-related DEGs (DECRRGs) were obtained by intersecting DEGs with curated CRRGs. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to identify AR-related gene modules. Machine learning algorithms, including support vector machine-recursive feature elimination and Boruta, were used to screen diagnostic biomarkers. Immune infiltration was assessed using CIBERSORT and single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis. Single-gene gene set enrichment analysis, non-negative matrix factorization-based molecular subtyping, and competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) network construction were subsequently performed. A total of 36 DECRRGs were identified and significantly enriched in immune- and inflammation-related pathways. WGCNA revealed a turquoise module that was strongly correlated with AR. Machine learning analysis identified two key diagnostic biomarkers, BTG1 and IDI1, which demonstrated robust diagnostic performance in both the training set (AUC = 0.781 and 0.755) and the validation set (AUC = 0.986 and 0.857). Immune infiltration analysis revealed significant alterations in immune cell composition between AR and control samples. Non-negative matrix factorization clustering classified AR patients into two distinct molecular subtypes with markedly different immune landscapes. Finally, a ceRNA regulatory network was constructed to elucidate the post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms of the diagnostic genes. This study systematically identified circadian rhythm-related diagnostic biomarkers for AR and revealed immune-based molecular subtypes, providing novel insights into the circadian-immune regulatory mechanisms underlying AR pathogenesis.

papers.title: The impact of sleep restriction on affective functioning in people with schizophrenia: an experimental digital phenotyping study.
papers.abstract: Previous reports indicate short sleep duration may have a detrimental impact of affective functioning. Sleep difficulties and negative affect are both ubiquitous among people with schizophrenia. However, there is scarce evidence linking the two in this population, with studies to date restricted to correlational and cross-sectional designs. To address this knowledge gap, we employed an experimental, within-person, cross-over design to characterize sleep duration and its affective sequelae in individuals with schizophrenia. Eighteen participants (average age = 37.67, SD = 9.47; 56% female), completed two overnight lab-based polysomnography examinations (at least two weeks apart) employing two sleep conditions: sleep restricted to a 4-hour opportunity (SR); and sleep over an 8-hour opportunity (control). Following each overnight sleep condition, participants completed three days of digital phenotyping of affective functioning via smartphones. On average, participants slept 3.35 (SD = 1.05) hours during SR, and 5.51 (SD = 1.81) during the control night. Following the SR, participants reported higher and significantly more variability of negative emotions, as well as increased negative impact of emotions on daily functioning, with particularly pronounced differences among individuals with lower alexithymia. Sleep condition was not associated with differential emotional granularity. Exploratory analyses indicated significant variability in use of emotion regulation strategies across the first, second-, and third-days post-sleep following SR, but not following the control night. This is the first study employing digital phenotyping via experimental design to examine the impact of sleep restriction on affective functioning. Our findings illuminate the critical role of sleep duration on affective experience and related daily functioning among people with schizophrenia.

papers.title: Simultaneous EEG-fMRI in major depressive disorder: A systematic review of brain networks, neurovascular coupling, and clinical correlates.
papers.abstract: Simultaneous electroencephalography-functional magnetic resonance imaging (EEG-fMRI) offers unique potential to characterize brain network dysfunction and neurovascular coupling in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, the field lacks a rigorous synthesis restricted to strictly defined MDD populations with true multimodal integration. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420261292902), we searched PubMed, Scopus, CENTRAL, and Google Scholar (inception to March 2026) for simultaneous EEG-fMRI studies in adults (≥18 years) with MDD. We excluded subclinical samples, healthy-only populations, and sequential acquisitions to ensure diagnostic specificity. Primary outcomes were network dysfunction, neurovascular coupling, and clinical associations. Narrative synthesis was performed due to data paucity (<3 studies/outcome). Risk of bias was assessed using modified ROB2, ROBINS-I, and JBI tools. Nine studies (eight cohorts; N=377) met strict criteria. Two reports from one cohort investigating anhedonia via neurofeedback (Zotev et al.) showed moderate-to-strong correlations between EEG-fMRI metrics and severity (r = 0.47 and 0.69). Single-study findings reported effect sizes for anxiety (r = 0.74), depression change (r = -0.38 to 0.90), and rumination (r = 0.20). Analytical heterogeneity was substantial. Evidence certainty was low due to bias risk and imprecision. Small sample sizes, methodological fragmentation, and reliance on single cohorts for specific outcomes limit generalizability. Simultaneous EEG-fMRI identifies strong neurophysiological correlates (e.g., anhedonia, treatment response) in active contexts (e.g., neurofeedback, ketamine), but evidence for generalizable resting-state biomarkers remains insufficient. Future efforts must prioritize standardized pipelines and large-scale cohorts to transition this technique to a clinical biomarker.

papers.title: Frontocentral theta oscillations bias perceptual judgments of ambiguous visual causality.
papers.abstract: Human perceptual decisions frequently rely on incomplete, ambiguous sensory inputs resolved prior to stimulus onset. Prior electrophysiological work confirms pre-event frontocentral ERP components predict ambiguous visual causal judgments, yet the spectrotemporal signatures of spontaneous oscillatory biases remain uncharacterized. Frontocentral theta signals proactive cognitive control, but whether pre-event theta oscillation modulates high-order causal inference independently of stimulus-locked ERPs remains untested. Thirteen volunteers (16 recruited, 3 excluded) completed a staircase-calibrated Michotte launching task with 64-channel EEG recorded. Time-frequency decomposition, permutation tests, and ERP-subtraction controls isolated pre-coincidence oscillatory patterns distinguishing causal bouncing and non-causal streaming percepts under PSE level. Elevated pre-coincidence Fz theta power robustly biased observers toward causal reports, showing a negative linear relationship between theta magnitude and streaming response ratios. The theta bias survived single-trial ERP removal, proving oscillatory signals carry predictive information distinct from known ERP markers. These findings imply frontocentral theta pre-allocates anticipatory cognitive resources to support intuitive causal reasoning, separating theta's executive regulatory function from alpha's modulation of basic sensory awareness. This study constructs a novel spectrotemporal framework explaining how spontaneous frontal oscillations sculpt ambiguous causal perception.

papers.title: Perioperative management of patients with recent concussion undergoing noncardiac extracranial surgery: A modified Delphi consensus study.
papers.abstract: Many patients present for surgery soon after concussion, when cerebral physiologic regulation may remain disturbed, and no evidence-based guideline or standardized consensus recommendations exist. We sought expert consensus for adults with recent concussion undergoing noncardiac extracranial surgery. We conducted a two-round modified Delphi study (November 2025-March 2026). Round 1 items, drafted from a systematic literature search, included case vignettes. Experts identified by bibliographic screening, directories, and nomination rated items on a five-point Likert scale; "do not know" responses were excluded from the denominator. Consensus was defined a priori as 75% agreement or greater, and strong consensus as 85% or greater. Thirty-five experts (33 anesthesiologists) from 17 countries completed both rounds; 13 of 16 Round 2 statements reached consensus. Agreement was unanimous for preoperative screening for concussion symptoms and neurologic red flags, and for avoidance of hypoxemia, abnormal carbon dioxide tension, sustained hypotension, and marked hypertension. Strong consensus supported generally deferring elective surgery until concussion symptoms resolve (97%), preoperative counseling (97%), structured follow-up (94%), and extended postoperative monitoring in higher-risk patients (91%). Consensus was not reached for regional anesthesia or monitored anesthesia care over general anesthesia (74%), electroencephalography-based depth of anesthesia monitoring (73%), or cautious long-acting neuraxial opioid use (69%). The panel did not define symptom resolution and established no symptom-independent waiting interval or concussion-specific numeric physiologic threshold. This anesthesiology-led consensus supports symptom-guided timing, physiologic stability, counseling, and structured follow-up; anesthetic technique, electroencephalographic monitoring, and neuraxial opioid use remain unresolved. The statements form an expert-informed framework, not an evidence-based practice guideline.

papers.title: Experimental design-guided deep learning for microscopy-based qualitative classification of assay-referenced glipizide powder-blend states: A proof-of-concept study.
papers.abstract: Microscopic imaging could complement conventional powder-blend analysis by providing a rapid qualitative signal from physical particle patterns. This proof-of-concept study examined whether 10× light-microscopy images can distinguish assay-qualified glipizide powder blends generated under contrasting mixing conditions. Five batches prepared by geometric dilution and ordered mixing and 25 batches prepared by short-duration direct mixing were retained after three independent powder samples per batch satisfied prespecified class-specific assay criteria. For the Mixed reference class, all three sample assays had to fall within 90-110% of target; for the Not Mixed class, all three had to lie outside this interval. The preliminary CNN comparison used 1802 original images (951 Mixed and 851 Not Mixed). Five pretrained CNN architectures, three input resolutions and four online augmentation levels formed a 60-configuration mixed-level factorial screen. DenseNet-121 with 1024 × 1024-pixel inputs and nominal 50× augmentation yielded the highest reported preliminary F1-score (0.9748; accuracy 0.9732). The methanolic UV reference method was linear over 5-60 μg/mL (R2 = 0.99998), showed negligible placebo interference, and gave 99.88-100.08% mean recovery across 80-120% spike levels. Continued image acquisition yielded a documented inventory of 3093 images (1438 Mixed and 1655 Not Mixed), partitioned into 2165 training and 928 validation images. Because batch-of-origin identifiers were not retained after class-wise image pooling, independently held-out batch performance could not be established. Post hoc Grad-CAM analysis on a reserved 120-image set showed representative attention within particulate regions without establishing chemical specificity or excluding protocol-associated morphology. MoGAPI assessment yielded a score of 81 for the proposed microscopy-CNN screening workflow versus 64 for the UV reference procedure. The findings support further evaluation of microscopy-assisted CNN classification as a complementary, reagent-minimized screening strategy rather than a replacement for validated quantitative analysis.

papers.title: Impact of Circadian Adaptation on Sleep Architecture and Neurobehavioral Performance in Simulated Shiftwork.
papers.abstract: Shiftworkers rarely achieve full circadian adaptation to their schedule. We studied the impact of circadian misalignment on sleep and neurobehavioral performance using a simulated shiftwork paradigm. Nineteen individuals (mean±SD, 38±10 yrs, 10F) were studied in an 8-day inpatient protocol with a Baseline day (8h sleep), followed by an abrupt 8-hour delay shift in sleep-wake timing maintained for four days (simulated shiftwork) paired with different ambient lighting conditions to promote circadian adaptation, then a 30-hour constant routine (CR). Circadian adaptation was measured using the change in Dim Light Melatonin Onset between Baseline and CR. Sleep was recorded by polysomnography; subjective sleepiness and neurocognitive performance were assessed at regular intervals. Daytime sleep following the final nightshift had significant reductions in total sleep time (TST), stage 2 sleep, sleep efficiency (SE), and an increase in wake after sleep onset (WASO) compared to Baseline (p<0.05). Greater circadian adaptation was significantly correlated with higher TST (r2=0.37, p<0.01), REM sleep (r2=0.37, p<0.01), and SE (r2=0.48, p<0.01), and less WASO (r2=0.53, p<0.01). More slow-wave sleep correlated with a higher PRM score and less sleepiness (both, p≤0.03). More circadian adaptation was associated with better sleep architecture, less sleepiness, and better neurobehavioral performance. Interventions to facilitate circadian adaptation, such as appropriately timed-light exposure, could improve sleep and performance in shiftworkers.

papers.title: Contactless Oxygen Desaturation Prediction and Oxygen Desaturation Index (ODI) Estimation from Nocturnal Breathing Sounds via Deep Learning.
papers.abstract: Intermittent hypoxemia is increasingly recognized as a stronger predictor of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) than the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). We developed a sound-based AI model to detect oxygen desaturation events and estimate the oxygen desaturation index (ODI) from nocturnal breathing sounds in a fully contactless manner. The model was trained using 2,973 nights of synchronized polysomnography (PSG) and audio recordings obtained from hospital- and home-based settings. Validation and independent testing were performed on 664 and 802 nights, respectively. Audio signals were converted into Mel spectrograms and processed using a Vision Transformer-based architecture. Performance was evaluated at the 30-second epoch level using sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 score, accuracy, and Cohen's κ. ODI estimation was assessed using Pearson correlation, Bland-Altman analysis, mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean square error (RMSE). For epoch-by-epoch desaturation detection, the model achieved a sensitivity of 0.79, specificity of 0.95, precision of 0.78, F1 score of 0.79, overall accuracy of 0.92, and κ of 0.74. Estimated ODI showed agreement with PSG-derived ODI (r = 0.93, R² = 0.87, p < 0.001). Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean bias of -0.29 events/h with 95% limits of agreement from -14.73 to 14.14 events/h. Breathing sound-based deep learning enables contactless detection of oxygen desaturation events and reliable ODI estimation. This approach may provide a scalable, non-contact method for sleep-disordered breathing assessment in real-world settings.

papers.title: Potter-Optimized Multiscale Bayesian Gated Axial Quantized Attention Network for Robust Multichannel EEG-ECG-Based Seizure Prediction.
papers.abstract: Accurate seizure prediction from physiological signals remains challenging because electroencephalography (EEG)-ECG recordings contain substantial noise, nonlinear temporal patterns, inter-subject variability, and complex cross-modal dependencies. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Potter-Optimized Multiscale Bayesian Gated Axial Quantized Attention Network (PM-BGAQAN) for robust three-state seizure prediction using multichannel EEG-ECG signals. The framework first employs adaptive weighted mean filter (AWMF) to suppress physiological noise while preserving relevant signal characteristics, followed by Convolutional Swin-Transformer Network (CSTN) for hierarchical multiscale spatiotemporal feature extraction and multimodal EEG-ECG representation learning. Inclusion of Bayesian Asymmetric Quantized Neural Network (BAQNN) is followed next for uncertainty-aware quantized features, whereas multiscale gated axial reverse attention (MGARA) exploits the discriminatory power of multiscale temporal dependencies using gated axial attention. Finally, Potter Optimization Algorithm (POA) optimizes the network parameters to improve classification performance and convergence. The proposed framework is evaluated using the Siena Scalp EEG dataset with timestamp metadata and the SeizeIT2 EEG-ECG wearable dataset for classification of preictal, ictal, and interictal states. Experimental results demonstrate an overall classification accuracy of 99.86%, whereas subject-independent validation achieves 98.06% average accuracy across the evaluated datasets. Ablation analysis further confirms the contribution of the individual components to the integrated framework. The results indicate that PM-BGAQAN provides an effective multimodal representation-learning strategy for robust seizure-state prediction and establishes a basis for future real-time, wearable, and clinically validated seizure monitoring systems.

papers.title: Balanced Block of hERG/Kv11.1, CaV1.2, and NaV1.5 in Proarrhythmic Risk Assessment: An Integrated Review of In Vitro Electrophysiology, In Silico Modeling, and hiPSC-CM Evidence.
papers.abstract: Drug-induced torsade de pointes (TdP) risk is commonly assessed by measuring inhibition of the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr), mediated by Kv11.1/hERG, together with QT-interval prolongation. These endpoints are sensitive but incompletely specific because concomitant inhibition of the L-type calcium current (ICaL) or late sodium current (INaL) can attenuate IKr-block-mediated repolarization delay. This narrative review evaluates balanced ion-channel block using recombinant-cell electrophysiology, in silico models, and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs). Potency ratios can describe relative channel inhibition but cannot alone establish a validated risk threshold or low clinical TdP liability. Concentration-response slopes, binding kinetics, unbound exposure, active metabolites, trafficking effects, and patient susceptibility also influence outcome. The CiPA-modified O'Hara-Rudy ventricular model and qNet-derived Torsade Metric Score are model-specific integrators rather than direct measurements of clinical repolarization reserve. The fixed-block simulations presented here illustrate interactions between inward and outward currents. hiPSC-CMs provide complementary functional evidence but remain limited by cellular immaturity and assay variability. The ICH E14/S7B Q&As (R1), adopted in August 2026, support integrated assessment and permit qualified alternative assays in defined contexts of use.

papers.title: Neurobehavioral Assessment of ADHD and Anxiety Co-occurrence in Pediatric Populations.
papers.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is frequently comorbid with anxiety, a condition that complicates diagnosis and treatment. Stimulant medications used to treat ADHD may exacerbate anxiety in some children, although this is not a consistent effect. This study investigates Alpha Peak Frequency (APF) as a potential neurophysiological marker, alongside Theta/Beta Ratio (TBR) and Sensorimotor Rhythm (SMR), to compare children with ADHD alone (ADHD group) and those with ADHD and comorbid anxiety (COM group) using electrophysiological and behavioral assessments. We assessed 98 children (8-16 years, M = 10.1, SD = 2.25) diagnosed with ADHD based on DSM-5 criteria, divided into ADHD (n = 46) and COM (n = 52) groups. Behavioral measures included the Conners' Parent Rating Scale-Revised (CPRS-R) and the Spence Children's Anxiety Scale (SCAS). EEG data were analyzed to compare APF, TBR, and SMR across frontal, central, and occipital regions. The COM group exhibited significantly higher SCAS anxiety scores but no significant differences in ADHD symptom severity compared to the ADHD group. EEG analysis revealed an overall reduction in APF in the COM group compared to the ADHD group, with multiplicity-adjusted post hoc comparisons confirming significantly lower APF at the central and occipital electrodes. Additionally, compared to the ADHD group, the COM group showed reduced SMR at the central site, lower TBR in the occipital region, and higher occipital beta activity. APF, TBR, and SMR differed between children with ADHD and COM groups. These group differences require replication, and their diagnostic or treatment-related relevance remains to be established.

papers.title: Longitudinal associations between perceived social support and maternal depression and anxiety across the perinatal period.
papers.abstract: Despite robust international evidence that social support protects maternal mental health, the role of social support across the perinatal period remains poorly understood in Aotearoa New Zealand. This study aimed to examine how perceived social support relates to maternal depression and anxiety during the perinatal period, comparing partner, family, and friend support, and testing whether stress and sleep moderate these associations. Participants were 121 pregnant women who completed monthly surveys over 12 months, including the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, Perinatal Anxiety Screening Scale, and Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support, along with measures of stress and sleep. Linear mixed models tested longitudinal associations and moderation effects. Higher perceived social support was consistently associated with lower depression and anxiety. Family support was the most reliable protective source. Stress predicted higher distress and moderated the effect of support on anxiety, with support being more protective under high stress. Sleep problems predicted greater distress but did not moderate support effects. Findings suggest that perceived social support, particularly from family, is an important protective factor for maternal mental health. Screening for social support and stress in perinatal care may strengthen early identification and guide family-centred interventions.

papers.title: Tirzepatide and inflammation: a critical reappraisal of the immunometabolic case for incretin-based therapy.
papers.abstract: Tirzepatide, a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, lowers high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) by 29-55% across randomised trials in obesity, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obstructive sleep apnoea, and interleukin-6 by 25-30% at 72 weeks. Much of this is not weight-mediated: in SURPASS-4 the fall in hsCRP correlated with that in body mass index at r = 0.07, and mediation analysis of trials of semaglutide, a selective GLP-1 receptor agonist, attributes only 21-62% of its hsCRP effect to change in glycated haemoglobin and/or weight. The mechanism, however, is not the one usually given: the account reproduced in most reviews, that incretin receptors on macrophages and T lymphocytes signal through cyclic AMP to restrain nuclear factor-κB, is not supported by the best-controlled data. The principal antibody used to detect the T-cell GLP-1 receptor gives signal in receptor-null cells; Glp1r is undetectable by quantitative PCR in peritoneal and adipose macrophages; and haematopoietic receptor deletion does not abolish semaglutide's anti-atherosclerotic effect. I therefore propose a three-route model, graded by evidence: limited direct signalling in a few validated lymphocyte populations, a central neuro-immune relay, and a large indirect metabolic contribution. That adipose macrophages are refractory to tirzepatide while Kupffer cells respond, and that C-reactive protein is hepatocyte-derived, suggest a substantially hepatic rather than adipose effect. Because the mechanistic evidence concerns GLP-1 receptor agonism almost entirely, the appraisal applies to incretin-based therapy as a class, tirzepatide being the worked example. Five falsifiable propositions are advanced with the experiments that would refute them.

papers.title: Characterizing the effects of phrenic nerve stimulation on ventilation during drug induced sleep endoscopy: a proof-of-concept study.
papers.abstract: Central sleep apnea (CSA) is characterized by cyclic breathing instability marked by recurrent apneas from absent diaphragmatic activity followed by compensatory hyperpneas. Although phrenic nerve stimulation (PNS) is an established therapy for CSA, current open loop stimulation algorithms may inadvertently intensify hyperpneas when stimulation coincides with intrinsic respiratory effort. This study aimed to explore the respiratory state-dependent effects of PNS. A proof-of-concept study using drug induced sleep endoscopy (DISE) in patients with obstructive sleep apnea as a physiological model. Continuous positive airway pressure was applied to maintain airway patency while airflow, tidal volume, and respiratory effort were recorded. PNS was delivered either during inspiration, augmenting intrinsic diaphragmatic effort, or during expiration, simulating stimulation during a central apnea. Ventilatory responses during stimulated breaths were compared with adjacent unstimulated breaths. Seven participants (mean age 57.3 ± 11.1 years; BMI 27.8 ± 3.9 kg/m²) completed the protocol. Expiratory-phase PNS generated intercalated breaths with markedly increased ventilation (mean 14.2 L/min (95% CI: [5.12, 23.19])) and tidal volume (120 mL (95% CI: [17, 223])), whereas inspiratory-phase stimulation produced more modest increases (7.4 L/min (95% CI: [1.84 ,12.89]) and 46 mL (95% CI: [-0.06, 0.16]), respectively). Variability in response was associated with the strength of diaphragm capture during expiratory stimulation but not during inspiratory stimulation. PNS demonstrates distinct respiratory state-dependent effects. It effectively restores ventilation when delivered during simulated central apnea but produces reduced or inconsistent effects when applied during intrinsic breathing. This physiologic insight supports the development of closed‑loop PNS systems that adapt stimulation timing to respiratory state to improve CSA therapy.

papers.title: Short-term physiological responses to nocturnal pressurization in male high-altitude workers: an exploratory pilot randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: This exploratory pilot randomized controlled trial investigated whether a nocturnal pressurization intervention, designed to simulate altitude reduction during sleep, was associated with changes in multi-system physiological responses in male workers with chronic intermittent high-altitude exposure. Twenty-four male workers were randomized to a Pressurization group (n = 12) or a control group (n = 12); Over a 5-week protocol, the Pressurization group slept at the simulated altitudes while both groups worked at 3500 m. The primary outcome was mean nocturnal peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2); secondary outcomes were ambulatory blood pressure (BP), serum normetanephrine and metanephrine, Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System components, and oxidative stress markers. The intervention was associated with short-term changes, the largest of which occurred during the 2000 m-simulated week. SpO2 was higher than in controls at 2500 m and 2000 m (both p < 0.001). Nocturnal diastolic BP was lower at 2500 m (- 7.25 mmHg, p = 0.024), normetanephrine, metanephrine and angiotensin II were reduced at 2000 m (Ang II: -23.10 pg/mL, p = 0.011), and 8-iso-PGF2α was lower with higher total antioxidant capacity at both altitudes. None of these differences persisted at the fifth-week recovery assessment. A nocturnal pressurization intervention simulating descent to 2000 m was associated with improved nocturnal oxygenation and short-term reductions in neurohormonal and oxidative stress in male high-altitude workers. The changes were reversible and had disappeared one week after the intervention ceased; they should therefore not be interpreted as an improvement in long-term adaptation, and the study should be regarded as hypothesis-generating.
papers.journal: International archives of occupational and environmental health

papers.title: Late Percutaneous Retrieval of a Septal Occluder to Facilitate Left Atrial Access.
papers.abstract: We describe intentional retrieval of a well-seated septal occluder device for left atrial access. A 28-year-old woman with platypnea-orthodeoxia and exertional desaturation down to 50% underwent patent foramen ovale closure. She developed refractory atrial tachycardia requiring left atrial mapping. Twenty days later, the device was retrieved percutaneously. Partial endothelization prevented resheathing, so the device and sheath were withdrawn together. The snare slipped in the inferior vena cava, and the device migrated into the main pulmonary artery before recapture and extraction. After multiple electrophysiology procedures, a Gore Cardioform occluder was implanted to preserve future transseptal access. This case demonstrates the technical challenges of retrieving a partially endothelialized occluder and the value of proactive device-control strategies. Device retrieval during early endothelialization can carry migration risk due to device stiffness; balloon stabilization may prevent it. Anticipating future transseptal needs should guide device choice at reclosure.

papers.title: Globus Pallidus Externus α-Band Activity Decreases After Deep Brain Stimulation in Clinically Responsive Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder Patients.
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the anterior limb of the internal capsule (ALIC) is an effective treatment for severe obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Identifying brain readouts of a positive response may guide further DBS optimization. We measured local field potential (LFP) changes from bilateral DBS leads in ten patients with OCD who were implanted at a uniform tractographic network target derived from prior DBS responders. We consistently stimulated dorsal lead contacts in the ALIC white matter while recording LFP from the ventral lead contacts in the grey matter of the anterior globus pallidus externus (GPe), a key node in the basal ganglia nonmotor indirect pathway. After six months of DBS, OCD symptoms decreased by 40% on average across patients, along with a significant decrease in α-activity across both hemispheres. Only one patient did not have an improvement in symptoms, and this was also the only patient who never exhibited a decrease in α in either hemisphere. Our findings suggest that therapeutic ALIC DBS coincides with a stable decrease in limbic-cognitive GPe α-power, which should be further investigated as a potential biomarker of sustained response.
papers.journal: Neuromodulation : journal of the International Neuromodulation Society

papers.title: The Europe-Asia-Pacific Divide in Atrial Fibrillation Management: Evidence, Practice, and Policy.
papers.abstract: Atrial fibrillation affects approximately 60 million people worldwide, and Europe and the Asia-Pacific region together carry most of that burden. This state-of-the-art review compares the 2 regions across 6 domains: epidemiology and risk factors, lifestyle and comorbidity management, stroke prevention, rhythm control and catheter ablation, digital health and artificial intelligence-electrocardiogram, and health system infrastructure and policy. Practice diverges in all 6. European management follows European Society of Cardiology guidelines, whereas Asia-Pacific region care varies across socioeconomic settings and rests on population-scale evidence, with region-wide guidance so far limited to topic-specific Asia Pacific Heart Rhythm Society (APHRS) consensus statements until the first APHRS guideline was released in 2026. Anticoagulation gaps have narrowed in both regions, yet disparities in financing, electrophysiology capacity, and digital access persist, and differences within each region rival those between them. Closing these gaps requires region-specific, resource-adapted strategies and mutual adoption of evidence generated in each region.

papers.title: [Digital media use and dependencies in adolescence: Psychological and mental health perspectives, regulatory dilemmas, and preventive considerations].
papers.abstract: Adolescents' digital presence is no longer merely a lifestyle phenomenon but a developmental, social-psychological, and mental health environment. Social media, short-video platforms, online gaming, and constant online availability have become major contexts for mood regulation, identity formation, peer embeddedness, and self-evaluation. This manuscript provides a narrative and integrative review of recent international and Hungarian literature. It discusses the psychological structure of problematic digital use, its mood-related, attentional, sleep-related, and interpersonal correlates, as well as regulatory and preventive issues from developmental, mental health, and phenomenological perspectives. The literature suggests that problematic digital use should not be equated with high frequency of use alone, but is better understood in terms of loss of control, functional impairment, and the outsourcing of affect regulation. In vulnerable adolescents, digital engagement may be associated with depressive and anxiety symptoms, poorer sleep, attentional instability, intensified social comparison, and increasingly externalized self-worth. Hungarian findings also indicate that digital media use is embedded in family and broader social ecology. Prevention and early intervention should not rely on a single restrictive or permissive policy measure, but rather on a coordinated system of platform responsibility, family and school containment, digital literacy, and early clinical recognition.
